title: The Udanavarga — the Sanskrit Dharmapada
attributionNote: The Sanskrit counterpart of the Pali Dhammapada, kept by the Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda schools; transmitted without an author as the Buddha's own verses collected under subject headings. GRETIL's e-text follows Franz Bernhard's edition (Göttingen 1965), which is based on the Central Asian manuscripts, and was input by Muneo Tokunaga.
description: The Udānavarga gathers the Buddha's awakening verses under thirty-three headings: impermanence, desire, anger, heedlessness, the wise and the fool, the sage, the awakened, suffering, the ending of craving, and the last section on the way to the deathless. Its verses are the close kin of those the Theravada schools chant — the pairs of the first chapter, the unfolding of the wise man's teaching, the elephant that bears the arrow, the wish-fulfilling jewel of the mind well-trained — here in the wording the Sanskrit schools transmitted and cited in their abhidharma literature.
historicalContext: The manuscripts of the Udānavarga recovered from Central Asia and the Gilgit region showed nineteenth and twentieth century scholars that the Dhammapada was not one book but a textual family, and Bernhard's edition is the standard critical text of its Sanskrit branch.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: all thirty-three vargas and their 944 verses, streamed from GRETIL at read time. Each passage is one verse, addressed as varga.verse. The e-text follows Bernhard's printed presentation, which separates the words of a verse with dots; the reader trims the e-text's own apparatus from the ends of a passage but keeps the edition's word separation. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
